summary:
Orbit Architect is an interactive, NASA-inspired 3D game that turns space-mission systems engineering into something players can experience. Players choose a science objective, select an orbit and destination, design a spacecraft from instruments, power systems, antennas, buses and launch vehicles, pass a flight-readiness review, launch, and receive a mission report. After a mission, they can tour the International Space Station or attempt a manual docking challenge.

The challenge asks for a game where players design, manage, and simulate a complete mission under real constraints. Orbit Architect does this with a pure engineering engine that checks mass, volume, power, bandwidth, budget, and risk. A seeded launch simulation makes outcomes reproducible, so good engineering can still meet bad luck. The report explains blockers, warnings, and failure causes, and compares the result with real-world missions.

It matters because students rarely get to feel trade-offs: more instruments raise science return but consume mass, power, and data capacity, and weak margins raise failure risk. Orbit Architect makes these relationships visible, replayable, and accessible through captions, keyboard controls, and reduced-motion support.
details:
What it does and how it works?

Orbit Architect is an interactive, NASA-inspired 3D game that lets players run a complete space mission, from idea to final report.

A player picks a science objective (climate monitoring, exoplanet observation, solar-weather monitoring, lunar ice surveying, or Mars science), selects an orbit and destination, and designs a spacecraft by choosing instruments, power systems, antennas, a spacecraft bus, and a launch vehicle.

A flight-readiness review then checks mass and launch capacity, spacecraft volume, power generation and consumption, communications bandwidth, budget, payload capacity, and mission risk, and lists any blockers and warnings. When the design passes, the player launches and watches a timed sequence of liftoff, orbital insertion, spacecraft deployment, cruise, and arrival.

The final report gives the outcome, score, engineering causes, risk effects, and comparisons with real-world missions. Afterwards, players can tour the International Space Station or attempt a manual six-degree-of-freedom docking challenge.

All mission calculations and the launch simulation live in a pure engine module, separate from the visuals. The simulation uses a seeded random-number generator, so the same design and seed always produce the same risk rolls, events, outcome, score, and cause chain. Results are transparent and re-playable instead of hidden behind unpredictable randomness.

Benefits

Players see that improving one mission characteristic can hurt another.

- More instruments increase science return but consume more mass, power, volume, and bandwidth.

- Higher orbits and deep-space destinations reduce available launch capacity.

- Weak margins raise the chance of failure, and good engineering can still meet bad luck, as in real spaceflight.

The game explains why each result happened, so players learn from both success and failure.

Intended impact

To give students and aspiring engineers hands-on experience of systems-engineering trade-offs that are usually taught only in theory, and to build intuition through experimentation and replay.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

- Languages: TypeScript, HTML, CSS

- Libraries and frameworks: React 18, Vite, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Drei, Postprocessing, Tailwind CSS

- Browser APIs: WebGL for 3D graphics, Web Audio API for procedural launch and spacecraft sounds

- Assets: GLB spacecraft and station models, planetary textures and normal maps

- Hardware: no special hardware; it runs in a modern browser with WebGL

How it is creative?

Orbit Architect makes systems engineering playable as a full lifecycle, and the deterministic seed turns luck into something players can inspect. A persistent 3D world (an operations base, a launch pad, and Earth, Moon, and Mars scenes) presents launch, orbit, cruise, and arrival as experiences instead of forms. The ISS tour and manual docking extend the game beyond mission design, and procedural sound, captions, and real-mission comparisons add depth.

Factors our team considered

- Energy: power generation and consumption are a core constraint in the game, and a quality-adaptation mode lowers the 3D load on modest devices.

- Accessibility: structured HTML panels, captions, keyboard controls, and a reduced-motion stylesheet.

- Simplicity versus realism: simplified calculations that keep realistic relationships between mission variables.

- Transparency: blockers, warnings, risk, score, and failure causes are all explained.

- Replayability: different objectives, designs, destinations, and seeds produce different outcomes.

- Maintainability: the engine is kept separate from the presentation layer.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

We used two SI tools in this project: Claude (by Anthropic) and GitHub Copilot.

Claude (Anthropic)

- Code generation: Claude generated code for the project, including the 3D scenes and the model animations.

- Planning and writing: Claude helped us structure the project plan, research NASA systems-engineering concepts, and draft our project summary and description.

GitHub Copilot

- Code refactoring: GitHub Copilot was used to refactor and clean up our code.

- Code documentation: GitHub Copilot was used to write code documentation.

Human oversight: Our team defined the game design and mission logic, and reviewed, tested, and edited the AI-assisted code and all submitted text.
